title: The works of mercy (CCC 2447)
hookLine: seven corporal and seven spiritual works

lines: WHEN DID WE SEE YOU HUNGRY?
cards: Jesus tells a story about the end of time. All the nations are gathered, and the king separates them, like a shepherd separating sheep from goats. To one side he says: come, you're blessed.
I was hungry and you fed me. I was in prison and you came to see me. They're baffled.
When? We never saw you hungry. We never visited you in prison.
And the king answers with one of the most quoted sentences in the Gospels. The Catholic Church took that story and turned it into two lists, seven and seven, that children still learn by heart.

teach.b: In the Douay-Rheims the king says: "Amen I say to you, as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." Catholics hear this as Christ hiding in the people who need something.

The first list is the corporal works, for the body. Six come straight from this story: feed the hungry, give drink to the thirsty, clothe the naked, shelter the homeless, visit the sick, visit the imprisoned.
The seventh, bury the dead, comes from the book of Tobit, where a man risks his life to bury his people's dead.
The second list is the spiritual works, for the soul. Instruct the ignorant. Counsel the doubtful.
Admonish sinners, gently. Bear wrongs patiently. Forgive offenses willingly.
Comfort the afflicted. Pray for the living and the dead. They're ordinary.
Teaching a kid to read counts. Sitting with a friend who's lost faith counts. Not forwarding the angry text counts.
And the word: in Latin, mercy is misericordia, from miser, wretched, and cor, heart, a heart that goes out to someone in misery.
The Catechism calls the works of mercy acts of charity by which we help our neighbor in their bodily and spiritual needs, and says giving to the poor is one of the chief witnesses to love.
Fourteen in all, and you don't have to do them all today.
Feed, teach, forgive: three of them fit in a single afternoon.

how: Catholic children often learn the seven corporal and seven spiritual works of mercy by heart, and parishes organize them through food pantries, hospital and prison visits, funeral ministries and prayer for the dead.

o: pity felt from a safe, comfortable distance
a heart that goes out to someone in misery
a pardon a judge grants to a guilty person

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: all fourteen works of mercy come from the sheep and goats story
six corporal works do; burying the dead comes from Tobit, and the spiritual works gather other teaching.
forgiving offenses is a work of mercy
forgive offenses willingly is one of the seven spiritual works.
mercy in Latin means a heart that goes out to misery
misericordia: miser, wretched, and cor, heart.

games.q: you're among the sheep. the king says: I was hungry and you fed me. you don't remember ever seeing him. what does he answer?
o: as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me.
it was a test, and you passed.
games.why: Christ is found in the least: whatever was done for them was done for him.

practice: Run through the fourteen slowly: feed, give drink, clothe, shelter, visit the sick, visit the prisoner, bury the dead; teach, counsel, correct gently, bear wrongs, forgive, comfort, pray.
One of them has a face attached, someone in your life right now, so stay with that face and picture the work in something small enough to actually do. If you pray, you can pray for that person.

wordCard.voice: Misericordia, the Latin word for mercy, a heart that goes out to someone in misery, behind the Church's fourteen works of mercy. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: mercy. from miser, wretched, and cor, heart.

carryVoice: Your line: feed, teach, forgive. Fourteen works, and every one of them has a face. That's day three hundred seventeen.
